summary: This informational document is a framework for time-scheduled reservation of traffic engineering resources. It can provide resource booking for TE LSPs, improving guarantees for customers and efficiency of network usage over time.

plainLanguage.summary: Reserving a meeting room for next week. This is a plan for booking network capacity ahead of time.

questions: how to book network resources in advance
how does a pce schedule lsps
why keep scheduling state in a central pce
subtitle: A framework for booking network tunnel capacity ahead of time, so a future path is guaranteed without wasting resources today.

tldr.problem: An operator often knows that a tunnel (an LSP) will be needed at a set time, but computing a path now gives no guarantee the resources will be free then, and setting the tunnel up early wastes them.
tldr.mechanism: A central Path Computation Element keeps a time-based view of network resources and a database of planned LSPs. It computes paths and books resources for future windows, and signals the LSP only when its start time arrives.
tldr.outcome: The RFC gives an architecture and design reasoning only. It defines no protocol or protocol extension, so the pieces must be realized elsewhere.

today: RFC 8413 is an Informational document from July 2018, and no RFC obsoletes or updates it. It describes an architecture and defines no protocol, so it is a reference for design rather than a specification to implement.

sections.title: Why Book Resources in Advance
sections.content:
Traffic Engineering Label Switched Paths (TE-LSPs) are connection-oriented tunnels that can reserve network resources, such as the capacity of a link. Network planning means choosing paths so that LSPs do not contend for the same resources.

Often it is known that an LSP will be needed at a specific time. Computing a path now does not guarantee the resources will be free later, yet setting the LSP up early is wasteful because the resources could be used for something else in the meantime. Time-Scheduled (TS) reservation of TE resources books them for a window in the future instead.

This document is a framework. It describes the problem and the architecture, and it does not describe specific protocols or extensions.
sections.plainLanguage: If you hold a seat at the cinema all week, nobody else can use it. If you just hope it is free on Friday, someone may take it. Booking a seat for Friday fixes both problems.

sections.title: The Problem with Planning Future LSPs
sections.content:
A requester may know that a large flow will start at a well-known time, for example a database synchronization or a content exchange between streaming sites, and for how long it will last. One approach is to hold such requests in a central database and ask a Path Computation Element (PCE) for a path when the time arrives. That can only be a best-effort guarantee, because other LSPs may use the resources in the meantime.

The better solution is to service future requests at once. Paths are computed ahead of time and turned into reservations during specific windows, but the LSP is not established in the network until its scheduled time.

Foreknowledge also helps in general. Placing LSPs one at a time can block later ones that would all have fitted if they had been known together. Unplanned LSPs can still be requested alongside scheduled ones. They are placed with the known future demands in mind, and since they have no known end time, planning assumes they use resources forever.
sections.plainLanguage: If the teacher knows every group that needs the big table this week, she can give each group a time. If groups just grab it as they come, some will find it taken.

sections.title: What State Is Kept, and Where
sections.content:
One piece of scheduling state is described as a link, a resource or reserved capacity, a reservation start time and a reservation end time. A reservation could instead be stored as a start time and a duration. One request may book several periods or a repeating cycle, and windows on a link may overlap.

The RFC weighs two places to hold this state. Keeping it in the network nodes makes policing easier, but every node would need the full time-based state, it would have to be advertised in the IGP, and it would be hard to recover after a node restart. Keeping it centrally brings its own issues, such as synchronizing several controllers and storing a lot of state. The conclusion is that the scheduling state should be held centrally at the point of use, not in the network devices.

The PCE therefore needs two stores. The first is a time-based Traffic Engineering Database (TED) holding, for example, unreserved bandwidth per link for a series of time intervals. The second is an LSP Database (LSP-DB) that records each planned LSP with its time interval, computed paths and reserved resources. The LSP-DB lets the PCE release the right resources if a request is cancelled or changed. The RFC notes that the scheduled TED can be recovered from the active network state and the scheduled LSP-DB.
sections.plainLanguage: The school keeps one big booking calendar in the office instead of asking every classroom to remember who booked what. It also keeps a list of the bookings themselves, so a cancelled booking frees up the right slot.

sections.title: The Reference Architecture
sections.content:
A Service Requester (an application, a network management system, an LSR or any Path Computation Client) asks the PCE for an LSP now or at a future time, supplying parameters such as priority, bandwidth, start time and end time. The PCE records the request in its LSP-DB, uses its TED to compute a path for the whole interval, and updates the TED with the future resource usage.

At the start time, the PCE sends a PCEP Initiate request to the head-end LSR with the path to signal. As the LSP is signaled, resource use is flooded in the IGP and shared with the PCE through the IGP or BGP-LS, and the PCE updates its TED. After setup the head-end sends a PCEP LSP State Report (PCRpt). When the LSP is cancelled or its lifetime ends, the PCE tears it down if active and removes it from the LSP-DB.

Depending on operator policy, the PCE may reoptimize LSPs after TED updates, issuing PCEP Update requests for provisioned LSPs or just editing the stored plan for those not yet provisioned. A starting or recovering PCE must learn the topology from the network, rebuild the time-based TED, and synchronize with other PCEs. The RFC lists options for that synchronization: a shared database, a distributed database mechanism, or PCEP messages.

Operator policy runs through all of this. Examples in the text are limiting the percentage of a resource that can be booked, and making preemption of booked resources depend on how far in the future they are first needed.
sections.plainLanguage: You tell the office what you need and when. The office writes it down and works out where everything fits. When the time comes, the office tells the right people to start, and then notes that it happened.

sections.title: Spanning Multiple Domains
sections.content:
A scheduled path that crosses several domains must book resources in every domain it crosses, so they are available when the LSP is finally signaled. The RFC compares three PCE cooperation methods.

  • Per-domain computation is not appropriate on its own, because downstream computation is triggered only by signaling. A similar scheme works if cooperating PCEs exchange PCReq messages for the scheduled LSP, optionally returning a path key.
  • Backward Recursive PCE-Based Computation (BRPC) can find a better end-to-end path, but suits scheduling poorly: the downstream PCE would reserve resources on all candidate paths and then release those not used.
  • Hierarchical PCE adds a parent PCE that coordinates the child PCEs, giving better visibility of the end-to-end path and better coordination of booking.
sections.plainLanguage: If your trip crosses two countries, you must book a seat in each one. A tour guide who talks to both booking offices for you makes that easier.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says scheduling leaves the protocol and signaling security implications unchanged from on-demand LSPs, and it points to the PCEP and signaling security documents it cites. Scheduling does widen the attack surface for a PCE-enabled TE system by giving an attacker a larger (logically infinite) window to initiate or plan an attack.

If bogus scheduled LSPs can be entered into the LSP-DB, a large number of LSPs could be launched and significant network resources blocked. The text therefore says control of scheduling requests needs to follow operator policy, additional authorization needs to be applied for access to LSP scheduling, and diagnostic tools are needed to inspect the LSP-DB for attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: If anyone could book the big table for the whole year, a prankster could block everybody. So only the right people may book, and someone checks the calendar for fake bookings.
